#7511. Trump administration asks Supreme Court to block lower court ruling keeping protected status in place for Venezuelan nationals

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The battle over the Temporary Protected Status program – which allows foreign nationals to remain in the United States and work here when they cannot safely return home – returned to the Supreme Court on Wednesday afternoon. Specifically, the Trump administration asked the justices to block a September 2025 ruling by a federal judge in San Francisco that kept the program in place for Venezuelans from going into effect. U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer told the court that if they do not act, the order by U.S. District Judge Edward Chen “will spring into effect, inflicting severe and immediate harm.”

Then-DHS Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas designated Venezuela for the TPS program in 2021 and again in 2023. In 2025, he announced that the program would be extended through October 2026. Mayorkas cited a “severe humanitarian emergency” resulting from the “severe political and economic crisis” in Venezuela as the reason for the designation.

After Mayorkas’ successor, Kristi Noem, announced her decisions to end Venezuela’s designation and its subsequent extension, a group representing TPS holders went to federal court in San Francisco to challenge those decisions. Chen set them aside, and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit upheld that ruling. In 2025, while that litigation was moving forward, the Supreme Court paused Chen’s order with regard to Venezuela, effectively clearing the way for the Trump administration to deport Venezuelan TPS beneficiaries while the case continued.

In June 2026, in Mullin v. Doe, the Supreme Court ruled – in a pair of cases involving Haitian and Syrian TPS beneficiaries – that courts generally cannot review the Secretary of Homeland Security’s decision to designate or terminate a country under the TPS program. Relying on that decision, the Trump administration asked the court to send the Venezuelan TPS case back to the 9th Circuit for another look, which the court did in October of this year.

When the case returned to the 9th Circuit, Sauer told the justices, and the Supreme Court’s initial stay of Chen’s ruling expired, the court of appeals entered an administrative stay, which is due to expire on Nov. 20. “Absent judicial intervention between now and” then, Sauer wrote, “the Department of Homeland Security will have to resurrect TPS status for hundreds of thousands of Venezuelans after a nineteen-month hiatus.” Indeed, he noted, his office “has been informed that the government could be forced to immediately release into the country some 1800 or so Venezuelan aliens from detention.” And all of this would result, he continued, even though the Supreme Court has already “conclusively held in Doe” that the TPS statute bars courts from reviewing the DHS secretary’s decision to designate or end the designation of TPS.

Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

#7505. Why Trade Desk Veteran Jed Dederick Joined The Startup ShopMy To Sell Creator Marketing

Jed Dederick has had an interesting view of the programmatic industry. He was a digital ads seller first at The Wall Street Journal and then WebMD until 2012, when he jumped across the exchange to the still-nascent DSP The Trade Desk.

The rest, as they say, is history. He eventually led all TTD sales as CRO, and had industry stage time as an expert witness throughout the Department of Justice’s publisher ad tech antitrust suit against Google.

But this month is Dederick’s first as CRO of ShopMy, a marketplace that connects marketers to social and online creators.

“In a world where the older forms of performance marketing like search are seeing massive declines and are in huge question,” creator content is ready to step up, he told AdExchanger.

We caught up with Dederick about the new role and how, practically speaking, social creator commerce can become an always-on paid performance channel.

DEDERICK: I have lots of experience with how ads have funded the distribution of content and information. The thing that stood out to me was how crowded and commoditized paid advertising has become.

[ShopMy] has this idea that there’s all of this value and performance locked up inside creator content. Brands see it with high conversion rates and success rates with individual creator relationships, but haven’t had real scale or measurability.

And I see a tremendous amount of untapped performance marketing value in the creator commerce world. I mean, for instance, if you’re interested in buying the best mosquito zapper, that’s easier now than it’s ever been.

The process of discovery, inspiration and purchase is happening inside the creator landscape. And there are huge pockets of individual value that haven’t been tied together.

Creators sign up for free, though we have to approve them. And they’re earning a commission on sales.

On the brand side, it’s a subscription model.

Anybody who’s worked on the brand side in creator influencer marketing knows it’s really painful to set up an individual relationship with a creator. The trade-off for that one relationship hasn’t always translated into a massive vehicle or a line item for performance marketing. And so what we’re doing is making it possible for a brand to reach thousands of valuable creators at once through one central place.

Does ShopMy have its own app or is it only plugged into affiliate networks and places where products are sold?

Our creators are putting up content in a lot of places [with affiliate marketing programs]. Meta is certainly one. Substack is one. TikTok is one. And understanding that creators have a lot of platforms to put out content, ShopMy is a central place for brands and creators.

Traditionally, brands have had to go to multiple places to manage individual creator relationships or rely on platform reporting from all the different places those creators can be. [ShopMy] is an easy way to gain promotion by creators without having to create individual, unique sponsorships with the creators.

And, I’ll also add, we’ve launched a shopper app very recently.

We’re doing $1.9 billion in GMV [“gross merchandise volume,” for the uninitiated] right now. So I think part of why this probably isn’t in the lexicon is that [ShopMy] has lived a lot in the commerce landscape, particularly in fashion and beauty.

But you can see why I look at this from a performance marketing lens and think, “Oh my goodness! If only the brands that I know and have worked with could run this way and think this way. This doesn’t need to just live in one pocket of the ecosystem.”

Who are you dealing with at an advertiser client? The “affiliate person” in the marketing org could be very different from the “performance marketing person.”

This is why I’m here. This is what I think is fun: busting up the old silos in the name of value and efficiency.

I mentioned that we have thousands of premium brand partners, like Jimmy Choo, for the sake of example. Those types of brands have had creator teams and affiliate teams, right? Sometimes they sit under PR. Sometimes it’s under the umbrella of social or paid media.

Brands have organized themselves that way because that’s been the opportunity so far. But what I do is I bring scale and liquidity that can make [creator content] basically a vehicle for what would have been performance marketing and paid media budgets.

In terms of working with hundreds of thousands of creators – orthodontists, baristas, airline stewardesses and endlessly on – how are they selling general stuff?

I think this idea is so much bigger than it currently is.

People’s social circles are how we’ve gotten trusted recommendations forever. Your friends or someone you trust in a field have given you recommendations, and those are way more powerful than anything you’ve gotten through paid ads.

There are people in our network across lots of disciplines who have their own followings in their fields. So, sure, in that case, that might be relevant for endemic brands. But an orthodontist might be relevant for oral care and personal care brands. Creators post lifestyle-oriented [content] across categories: be it travel, fashion, cosmetics.

The reality of this landscape is how we get recommendations that used to be from our friends, maybe a co-worker, someone from a group chat. That’s the basis for what we’re scaling with creators.

Is there a brand safety/verification-type partner?

The reality is that how we think of user-generated and quote-unquote “premium” content is less helpful now. I don’t know about you, but when I go home, I turn on Netflix, and I see YouTube creators on Netflix. What my family’s watching is YouTube creators on Netflix with longer-format shows.

The world has changed quite a bit. There’s authentic content that connects, and there’s everything else.

#7501. Going Straight To The C-Suite; All I Want For Christmas Is Hess Truck Ads In September

Pinch your nose and blow gently through your nostrils.

That’s how to unpop your eardrums on a plane, or after taking the elevator from the lowly marketer offices to the executive floor.

Earlier this month, this newsletter noted the trend of holdco CEOs making handshake deals with brand CEOs to poach accounts their agencies didn’t even pitch. That’s the theory behind Publicis landing PepsiCo, Microsoft and LVMH.

Deloitte Digital is another example, as Digiday reports. The marketing consultancy arm of Deloitte’s holdco is going straight to CEOs to pitch its new enterprise operating system.

Traditionally, the marketing department has been Deloitte’s target and entry point. But the kind of enterprise deal it’s now seeking requires CEO approval and is part of a “more executive conversation,” says Deloitte Digital US CMO Mark Singer.

Plus, Deloitte’s product is called Converge Front Office (or “CFO,” lol).

The product name is fitting, as Gartner VP Jay Wilson perhaps unwittingly notes, since CFOs are taking bigger roles in evaluating marketing spend: “Increasingly, we see and hear from clients and agencies that the CFO is the critical piece of the new business puzzle, as marketing budgets remain flat.”

Deloitte Digital’s thinking is that brands have archives of back-filled content, copy and campaigns that haven’t been touched in ages. So why not have AI agents upcycle that content instead of buying more?

Gotta hand it to them; it’s definitely not a holdco pitch.

It’s not just you – the Christmas creep started creeping even earlier this year.

This September, there were 11% more holiday-themed ads on TV than in 2025 and six times more than in 2021, according to Nielsen.

Not surprisingly, retailers are on track to spend the most of any ad vertical. They made up almost 64% of all holiday ads aired on linear TV in October, which actually outpaces their usual holiday ad blitz. Over the past five years, retail accounted for about 45% of holiday ads across both linear and streaming TV.

Nielsen also notes some historical trends that could factor into this holiday season. For instance, there were a lot more automotive holiday ads on streaming (18.4%) than there were on linear (9.7%) last year. Maybe it’s a way to appeal to cord-cutting millennials who’ve started saying “Happy Honda Days” to each other as a bit.

But does running holiday ads sooner get consumers to spend more throughout the season?

According to Deloitte’s annual holiday shopping survey (which was conducted between late August and early September), the average household spend will increase 4% to $1,654 this year. And, while 22% of consumers plan to shop earlier this year, they expect 28% of their budgets to be spent by the end of October – the highest share Deloitte has seen in six years.

So total holiday spending may be up a bit. But it won’t pay to wait until Mariah Carey is fully thawed to run those ads.

The global internet is getting less global. And questions that once seemed outright crazy – such as, “Might Meta stop doing business in the European Union?” – are not so crazy anymore.

There’s no urgent crisis for Meta. The canary in the coal mine is really X. Elon Musk has threatened to stop serving X users in Europe going back to 2023 and fumed over a $140 million Digital Services Act fine last year.

But as Eric Seufert notes at Mobile Dev Memo, there’s a confluence of problems in Europe for Meta that could force its hand.

The EU’s anti-personalization rules and requirement that Meta offer an ad-free subscription service have also decreased the platform’s advertising payouts.

Plus, the European Commission’s Digital Fairness Act is taking shape. It would prohibit common mobile game monetization tactics like offering virtual in-game currencies or letting users pay for “variable-reward systems” (aka loot boxes). If mobile games make less money in the EU, that means smaller budgets for mobile app advertising, which is a revenue pillar for Meta.

At some point, these things add up. And, eventually, staying in the EU may not make mathematical sense for Meta.

#7496. Websites Aren’t Just For People Anymore. Here’s How Marketers Optimize Them For Agents

It’s always nice for a marketer to get a compliment on their website. But does the compliment still resonate when it comes from an AI agent?

Ask again in a few months and we might have an answer.

The product builds on its existing AI marketing solution, Ace, but is specifically focused on making website content more accessible to AI agents.

But what does it mean for content to be accessible to agents that, by definition, can access pretty much all content across the web?

Effectively, it involves reformatting content into simpler terms and unifying it from multiple sources onto a single webpage, said Andrew Bolton, chief customer officer at Knotch.

Most LLM crawlers declare themselves when they access a webpage, so Knotch knows to show them the AI version of a page, said Bolton. For those that don’t declare, Ace can analyze actions like on-site behavior to determine that the viewer is a bot.

AI agents, unlike humans, don’t care about interactive features or aesthetically pleasing graphics. Instead, their focus is on brevity and direct statements.

Often, the reformatting includes adding FAQs and concise summaries, as well as removing JavaScript. The result is a pared-down version of the webpage a human would see, but the key content remains.

That’s what Bolton describes as a one-to-one version of an existing webpage, in which the information that’s already on it is simply restructured, but nothing new is added. That’s one of the two types of pages that Ace for Agents can develop – the simpler, “v1” offering, said Bolton.

The slightly more advanced version of Ace for Agents involves “injecting new components of information” from other sources of the brand’s choosing, he said, like third-party review sites, or the brand’s own YouTube channel.

For instance, he added, if a car manufacturer had a particularly favorable review on a third-party site comparing one of its models to a competitor’s model, Knotch can ingest that into the manufacturer’s context model.

Reviews “would be valuable to a consumer who’s trying to evaluate those two different vehicles,” he added. Marketers have a say on whether they want to manually flag external reviews and other content to pull in, or if they want to use an agent to automatically pull in new, positive content, which a human can then review.

The resulting webpage is a “super piece of content” that is able to “combine the atoms” of several different pages across the web, said Bolton. Now, an LLM only needs to access one page, but gets the same amount of data that it historically would’ve collected from crawling all of the data sources individually.

It’s worth noting that the data inputs are entirely curated by the brand. In other words, the good reviews will be ingested, and the bad ones won’t. A brand wouldn’t elect to put negative reviews on their website, Bolton said, and Knotch is effectively creating an agent-readable webpage that pulls all of the informative and positive information on the brand into a single source.

As marketing and the open web rapidly evolve, agencies need to build an “experience that reaches both the people and the machines,” Melissa Berger, chief solutions officer at Digitas, told AdExchanger. “Earning attention” has always been a major focus for the agency, Berger said, “and now that’s not just earning from the human; it’s earning from the agents, too.”

Digitas has been working with Knotch for over a year and began testing Ace for Agents several months ago as a way to earn some of that agentic attention.

Although Ace for Agents has been a good way for brands to increase discoverability, they still need to understand who their human customers are, said Berger. Otherwise, the LLM-accessible site may be full of information, but not have the answers to the specific questions the humans are looking for.

Once a brand understands exactly what sort of questions its customers are asking and what queries it should aim to show up against, said Berger, “the rest of the content is updated to be catered more toward that.”

#7494. Ad Tech Doesn’t Need Another Tool. It Needs Fewer Handoffs

Every few months, we get excited about an industry update, like a new ad format or AI tool. That energy is a big part of what keeps ad tech moving forward, but I believe the next five years will be shaped less by any single innovation and more by how well the tools we already have work together.

The marketing technology landscape has 15,384 solutions and counting. The opportunity now is in the gaps between them, because that’s where time, data and trust get lost.

Think about a typical day for an affiliate. They usually juggle several platforms to find offers and buy traffic. And when it comes to site or landing-page monetization, that can mean yet another platform. On top of that, they have to keep track of balances and compare reports.

Together, these tools power decisions about budgets and traffic. But every handoff takes time, and some data inevitably gets lost along the way.

Agencies feel it, too. At POSSIBLE earlier this year, the conversation turned to whether AI can finally break down those silos and perhaps eliminate a few steps along the way.

The most important handoff in any AI workflow is the one from data to decision. AI can generate advertising copy and visuals very quickly at scale. But it can also optimize areas outside of the creative process: identifying outliers, explaining why a campaign behaves as it does, suggesting improvements, matching traffic with the right offers and taking over repetitive tasks.

What we don’t discuss enough, however, is that AI is only as good as the data it works with. If the data is flawed or weak, all AI can do is help you make the wrong decision faster. Before automating decisions, it’s worth making sure you can trust the data.

Some of the riskiest handoffs are the ones we don’t control at all, especially our dependence on platforms that can change the rules overnight.

Changes like these will keep coming. However, there is something we can do: Build businesses that adapt quickly. When the parked-domain change happened, RollerAds didn’t start from scratch; we adapted the traffic monetization infrastructure we already had to work with domain traffic. In my experience, that’s what most real innovation looks like: spotting a shift early and building on what you already do well.

The last handoff is between partners, and it only works if both sides trust what they’re seeing.

Advertisers need to trust their partner platform and the traffic this platform provides. Publishers need to be able to predict their earnings. Affiliates need their conversions reported accurately. A great interface makes all of this easier to see, but what earns trust is what’s underneath: reliable tracking, fraud protection and clear, honest communication.

If I could ask the industry for one thing, it would be to make ad tech understandable.

At its core, the idea of digital advertising is simple: Show people relevant ads. But, over time, it has grown into a complex mix of acronyms, integrations and dashboards.

Here’s my invitation to every platform: Before shipping the next feature, count the handoffs it removes. That’s the thinking behind RollerAds as a full-cycle ad platform. We’ve brought buying traffic, monetizing sites and running offers together in one account, and we keep looking for more steps to remove. The next big thing in ad tech may not be a thing at all. It will be the stage when tools combine into one seamless process with fewer handoffs, data we can trust, businesses that can absorb change and partners who make hard things simpler.

#7490. Disney Touts Its Streaming Success In Latest Earnings

After a lot of internal upheaval and consolidation, the House of Mouse finds itself in a pretty good place going into its fiscal 2027 year.

So says new CEO Josh D’Amaro and CFO Hugh Johnston during an earnings call on Tuesday. They told investors that Disney exceeded its guidance for the previous quarter and is on track to exceed its three-year adjusted earnings-per-share growth guidance going into the new year.

For the full year, revenue not only increased 8% but broke the $100 billion mark, from $94 billion in the fiscal year 2025 to $102.3 billion in 2026.

Meanwhile, for Disney’s Q4 (the company starts its fiscal year a quarter earlier), revenue increased 16% to $25.9 billion for last quarter, compared to $22.5 the year before.

Within entertainment, advertising grew 10% to $1.7 billion. And SVOD revenue increased 19% to $6.1 billion, with 22% subscription revenue growth.

In TV, D’Amaro highlighted the critical buzz around Hulu’s crime thriller “Furious,” high ratings for the new season of “Dancing with the Stars” and excitement over “The Remarried Empress,” a South Korean romantasy that debuted as the biggest premiere for a local original across Disney+ and Hulu globally. The latter is indicative of Disney’s plan to invest more in international content, a strategy that’s been working wonders for competitors like Netflix.

Sports are also a big deal, of course. Subscription and affiliate fee revenue in the sports segment increased 18% in the quarter to $3.4 billion, with advertising revenue growth of 20%.

Disney will continue to grow its sports footprint next year with expanded college football rights, increased “Monday Night Football” ratings and ESPN’s first ever Super Bowl telecast. (Well, technically, it’s ABC’s turn to host the Big Game, but it’ll also be cross-broadcast on other Disney channels.)

Where Disney’s overall streaming strategy is concerned, D’Amaro told investors that there will be a larger focus on “connecting services” – which includes other nonentertainment sides of the business like parks, cruise ships and merchandise.

More practically, though, “connecting services” means finally unifying Disney+ and Hulu into one app, which D’Amaro said would start in December. It also means adding more sports content to Disney+ and introducing creator content from TikTok into the Disney+ mobile app next month. The move might strike some as strange, but given that ESPN’s short-form Verts product broke records in September and October, maybe there’s something to it.

At the same time, Disney is still exploring the idea of a free streaming product, which leadership first discussed during last quarter’s earnings reports.

Despite – or maybe because of – all the streaming success, Disney announced it will stop reporting its SVOD operating income beginning next quarter. At the same time, the company will also provide additional disclosures related to revenue within the entertainment segment.

SVOD revenues will still be reported, Johnston clarified to investors, but so will content and IP revenues. Revenue for linear networks will be combined with the virtual MVPD business.

The goal, said Johnston, is to provide investors with “additional information and a better lens into our content monetization,” while allowing Disney’s team more flexibility to “invest appropriately” in growing SVOD.

In other words, Disney’s likely planning to spend a lot more money on its SVOD business – and maybe it doesn’t want investors to worry too much about how the sausage is getting made.

Disney’s remarkable growth this past quarter isn’t surprising, given how much the company has restructured since D’Amaro took on the CEO role in March. At least 1,000 members of Disney’s workforce have been laid off since then, with more job cuts and consolidation reportedly on the way.

All that streamlining is expected to translate into $3 billion in run rate savings by 2029, according to D’Amaro.

To highlight the ways Disney is prioritizing efficiency and consolidation, D’Amaro also shouted out the company’s first ever chief technology officer, Karandeep Anand, who came from the (now bankrupt) chatbot startup Character.ai.

Not surprisingly, Disney plans to continue investing in AI tools and technology across its entire business, even parks. Although D’Amaro didn’t bring up the company’s recent purchase of Character.ai’s assets, he did hype up how the tech is being used in the streaming side of the business, both within Disney+’s content recommendation engine and in the advertising products Disney makes available to its marketing clients.

In addition to Disney’s AI creative studio that uses existing brand material to develop CTV-ready ads, the company also launched an agentic ad campaign tool in August. Both were previewed at its tech and data showcase at CES earlier this year.

Now, almost half of all new ad campaigns are flowing through the agentic tool, according to Disney’s ad sales team.

#7487. X offers to let creators chill–it’ll pay clippers for them, and give them a kickback too

Everyone is competing for creators’ attention lately–but X has been doing it for years.

Its latest bid: a clipping tool that pays both creators and clippers for reposting bite-sized pieces of longer content.

“Grab your favorite moment from any video, add your take, and post it without leaving X,” the platform said in a company post. “Creators: every clip credits your original video and links back to it, so new viewers can find your work and keep watching. Clippers: you now have an easy, native way to share moments from your favorite creators directly on X. The best part? Both the original creator and the clipper can earn from views on the clip through Original Content Rewards. Everyone wins when great moments travel.”

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

As you very likely know, clipping is the method du jour for creators to spread the word about their stuff. Sometimes fans clip for free/for the love of the game, but in many cases, creators pay people to clip their long-form videos and spread the shorter vids across platforms, hoping to drive more people to their full-length YouTube videos, Twitch streams, or podcast episodes.

With its clipping tool–which, from the announcement video, looks like a basic trimmer with no real editing capabilities–X is telling creators, Hey, you don’t have to worry about hiring clippers for our platform. We’ll do it. That could be an upside for creators who don’t want to compensate people themselves.

Grab your favorite moment from any video, add your take, and post it without leaving X.

Creators: every clip credits your original video and links back to it, so new viewers can find your work and keep watching.

Clippers: you now have an easy, native way to share moments from your favorite creators directly on X.

The best part? Both the original creator and the clipper can earn from views on the clip through Original Content Rewards.

Everyone wins when great moments travel. Clipping is one more step toward making X the best place to create, grow and earn.

And for clippers, the upside is financial. Clippers who aren’t directly hired/otherwise greenlit by creators generally don’t make money off their reposts, since reuploaded material can be (and usually is) copyright claimed by the original creator. A successful claim will divert any earnings to that creator. Makes sense, since it’s their content.

X, however, is offering a blanket green light. We’re not sure Elon Musk‘s platform will pay enough to tempt pro clippers, but it might appeal to aspiring clippers who seek a lower barrier to entry.

To be clear, though, we don’t know how much X will pay clippers. It says they’ll earn money through its rewards program, which pays a set amount based on engagement metrics, but how will revenue be split between creator and clipper?

Also worth noting: Not everyone can join the rewards program. X has to approve you first.

Like we mentioned above, this is far from X’s first attempt to woo creators. Not long after Musk bought it, X (still called Twitter at that point…RIP) increased its max video length to 60 minutes, clearly hoping to pull some YouTubers. Musk himself personally appealed to MrBeast, who obliged and put a long-form video on X in early 2024; he did not seem overly impressed by the results, and has stayed firmly on YouTube, where he’s the biggest fish around.

Other tweaks X has made include abolishing Twitter’s iconic character limit (thus attempting to challenge YouTube text posts as well as newsletter hubs like Substack), letting creators paywall posts, and adding a “completely redesigned livestreaming control room.” That last launch came with a promise to shell out a total of $1 million to streamers who went live on X.

#7485. Stop Hunting for Hang-Gliding Nuns. Your Local CTV Campaign Needs Scale.

Premion’s Head of Pricing and Planning, Adolfo Arbulú, on why hyper-targeting suffocates local CTV campaigns, and why AI still requires a human in the lead.

It is easy to get seduced by the promise of hyper-targeting in connected TV.

But stacking audience filters—like trying to reach “hang-gliding nuns who drink energy drinks”—creates a massive problem for local advertisers: it shrinks the available pool of households down to virtually zero.

In this episode of Inside the Stack, Premion’s Head of Pricing & Planning, Adolfo Arbulú, joins the podcast to untangle the Local CTV Paradox.

He explains why true precision actually depends on scale, and why chasing that scale across multiple unmanaged CTV partners creates massive frequency overlap and hidden waste.

We also dig into the reality of AI in local markets. For a local campaign generating a few dozen conversions a week, relying on hourly AI optimization simply creates noise.

Arbulú also shared why campaign measurement must be decided well before the buy, how Premion is using a proprietary identity graph to control frequency, and why navigating local nuances—like unexpected town layoffs or mid-term political cycles—means AI still desperately needs a human in the lead.

#7482. Have you heard? MatPat’s return, Tubi CEO’s next move, and Trisha Paytas’ payday.

Each week, we handpick a selection of stories to give you a snapshot of trends, updates, business moves, and more from around the creator industry.

This week, a beloved couple has a new channel on YouTube, a vaunted exec has a new gig, and a much-memed creator is making bank (and hitting bookshelves).

Welcome back to YouTube, Matthew and Stephanie Patrick. The man known as MatPat and his wife Stephanie haven’t shared many videos since they sold their Theorist brand nearly four years ago. But these crazy kids couldn’t stay offline forever, so they’re back with PatChat, a new channel featuring the couple’s conversations about internet culture. PatChat won’t upload nearly as frequently as the Theorist channels, and that’s ok. Let the Patricks live a little bit!

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

CNN panelist pushes back against Hasan Piker lawsuit. Piker argued that Scott Jennings defamed him by misconstruing statements that were clearly said in jest. In response, Jennings’ lawyers argued that Piker did make those statements, sarcastic or not — so they are looking to have the $72.5 million lawsuit thrown out. If commentators can be held liable for sarcasm, the internet might be in real trouble.

WhatCultureGaming launches new YouTube channel to pursue different types of content. After building a popular gaming hub, the WhatCulture team is trying something a little different with MegaWhat. The plan is to release original, personality-driven content that will give the WC team more creative freedom while still allowing them to feed the YouTube algorithm on their main channel.

Anjali Sud leaves Tubi to take point at SiriusXM. As CEO of Tubi, Sud led the transformation of the Fox-owned service, which is now a major creator hub. (She was also CEO of Vimeo before that.) Now, Sud is becoming CEO of SiriusXM, giving her a chance to work her magic in the realm of digital radio. Mike Bidgoli will take over for Sud as the new top exec at Tubi HQ.

Elevate Communications brings in TikTok vet to expand creator operations. Elevate is elevating Sam Valentine, who previously connected TikTok with luxury fashion brands as the app’s Head of Digital, Social, and Creator Services. He’ll spearhead digital and social partnerships at Elevate, where he will work with clients that are eager to build creator programs in sectors like sports, entertainment, and healthcare.

Meta brings in well-traveled exec to be the VP of its in-house content studio. After a long stint at NBC News, as well as stops at Goldman Sachs and BlackRock, Rich Latour has arrived at Meta. He will be put in charge of a studio that emphasizes Meta’s brand and highlights its impact across various communities and industries.

Trisha Paytas has a book out (and she makes $100,000 a week on YouTube). While promoting her memoir Crying on the Kitchen Floor, which was recently published by Hachette, Paytas told Andy Cohen that her YouTube earnings can hit six figures during a good week. Oh, and she also has a new dating show that is rolling out on Tubi. Slow down, Trish!

Hulu taps Tinx to revive The Circle (now with TikTok voting). The creator born Christina Najjar is taking the hosting role in a new version of the reality competition series that previously aired on Netflix. Tinx will have big shoes to fill replacing previous host Michelle Buteau, but with help from the voting audience, she can ensure that the Circle revival doesn’t miss a beat.

The first Clio Creator Awards will fete Dhar Mann. Actor Terry Crews will host as the notable advertising award ceremony expands to the realm of creator content. Dhar Mann, YouTube moralist and engineer of many a brand partnership, will receive an inaugural honorary award at the new ceremony.

Kind works with a Savannah Banana to sell a TikTok-exclusive foodstuff. Baseball player Jackson Olson has amassed a significant TikTok following after getting a roster spot on the best-known “Banana Ball” team. Olson is now parlaying his influence to sell a new type of Kind bar that celebrates World Kindness Day — and is only available for purchase via TikTok Shop.

GTA VI codes are flying around on Kick and Twitch ahead of launch day. All of the major platforms want creators to play GTA VI on their services once the game launches, and giving out free copies is a good way to engender that loyalty. At this point, I’m wondering if GTA VI will be able to live up to its immersurable hype, or if viewers will tire of it after it because the main topic of conversation everywhere.

Barbie and Hot Wheels are on TikTok Shop this holiday season. TikTok continues to onboard name brands as it prepares for its most lucrative holiday season shopping spree. So if someone on your list has their eyes on some Mattel products, deals on those items will be hitting TikTok Shop in no time.

Celebs are consenting to having their voices cloned for AI ads. Ogilvy and CAA have teamed up for a partnership that will make a-list talent more accessible for advertisers and agencies that rely on generative AI pipelines. George Clooney is a CAA client, but if he goes along with this, I’m going to have no choice but to start calling him George Cloney.

Shaq is good at dunking, but can he hide in plain sight? The Big Diesel has a new gig: An ABC series that will ask contestants to hide the 7’1″ goliath in plain sight. I think, to be fair, the contestants should get to start by hiding Kevin Hart before working their way up to Shaq.

Another impulse spending deterrent is taking off in China. The WeChat mini-app dubbed ‘Wallet, Please Wait’ lets users decide whether strangers will be able to hold off on big purchases. I would be more interested in app that lets me vote on whether a stranger should be able to tell a stranger how to spend their money.

#7480. Meta Makes Its Way To The Big(ish) Screen; Fubo’s Fraught Q3

YouTube has become TV, video podcasts are following suit and now Meta is looking for its way into the living room.

Meta has already been testing Instagram for TV built around long-form creator content. But it could make a bigger splash in the TV world through the acquisition of a CTV startup or a streaming company so Reels are “front and center on TV screens,” Mike Shields suggests in his Next in Media Substack.

If Meta wants to compete with Google and Amazon, acquiring, owning and operating are probably paramount (no pun intended). “Audience alone won’t be enough,” Dan Larkman, CEO and founder of performance CTV tech company Keynes, tells Shields.

But others argue that bringing Instagram to TV doesn’t require acquisitions – just Meta investing to build out its own existing features.

And perhaps Meta agrees. According to Shields, citing sources familiar with the discussions, Meta is talking with TV OEMs and FAST platforms about adding an “extend to CTV” option to its ad-buying platform.

Speaking of TV, Fubo’s quarterly earnings report card was a mixed bag.

The sports-centric streamer saw overall revenue inch up ever so slightly to $1.5 billion last quarter, compared with $1.48 billion during the same period last year. But it suffered a heavy net loss of $51.8 million last quarter, compared with $38.8 million a year ago.

The streamer blames operational and restructuring costs related to its recent merger with Hulu + Live TV for most of its recent losses. Going forward, it’s betting on advertising and live sports distribution (surprise, surprise!) to save the day under its new CEO Alisa Bowen.

And ad revenue is already moving in the right direction.

Bowen also told investors that the company plans to keep aggregating sports content rather than investing in sports rights, which are not getting any cheaper. However, some analysts believe that content IP ownership – including for sports – is more valuable as a competitive differentiator compared with distributed content. (Ruh-roh.)

Guess sports alone aren’t enough to keep Wall Street happy.

The internet opened up access to information. AI is helping big platforms close it back down.

Google is starting to put up barriers to its search results. It’s testing a prompt that asks users to sign in to verify they’re human, Search Engine Roundtable reports. The prompt appears when Google suspects a bot is scraping its results.

The same barriers are appearing on Google Maps and business reviews, since reviews contain such rich data on particular products and customer intent. Meanwhile, OpenAI has done the same thing with its results so rival bots can’t scrape and reverse engineer its outputs.

Oh, and Meta is running campaigns to get users to download Muse, its AI agent, as a Chrome extension. This could help Muse get around bot detection tools used by publishers and retailers like Amazon and eBay.

Finally, Reddit was built around the notion of transparency and free access, so it was a big change last month when it removed public API access and the free feed.

The FBI flags Gootloader, a malware campaign that used more than 1,000 compromised WordPress sites and SEO tricks to lure users into downloading malware disguised as business documents. [Search Engine Roundtable]

Instagram (finally) lets creators add Amazon affiliate links directly to Reels and feed posts. [TechCrunch]

Creative agency Saylor appoints Sarah McMains as chief strategy officer. [release]

#7477. Philips Sonicare Polishes Its Streaming TV Strategy Using Amazon Ads Agent

Brushing your teeth is a chore, and so is trying to buy streaming TV ad inventory publisher by publisher.

During the 2025-26 upfront season, Philips Sonicare, a maker of electric toothbrushes and water flossers, decided to consolidate its streaming TV ad buys within Amazon, which has also been doing some consolidating itself. Amazon recently centralized its Amazon DSP has been replaced by a new product called DVA+ (which stands for “display, video and audio”).

In both cases, the rationale for consolidation is simplification. When media workflows merge, ad transactions need fewer dashboards and third parties, which improves campaign efficiency and performance.

Philips Sonicare, which was already using Amazon’s Sponsored Ads to market its products on the flagship site, but wanted to expand its target audience after finding that 86% of the oral care audience segment was not considering Philips products.

To reach them, the brand paired Amazon’s data with its own first-party data to create custom audience segments of customers who are in market for oral care products but haven’t shopped from Philips before.

As part of its upfront commitment, Philips used Amazon Ads Agent to buy streaming media across Paramount+, Roku, Tubi, Peacock, TelevisaUnivision and Warner Bros. Discovery. Previously, it had to work with each of these publishers separately.

By consolidating its buys, Philips saw 24% incremental reach it saw among audiences likely to be interested in its products, as well as a 75% reduction in customer cost per acquisition.

For brands, centralizing multi-platform streaming buys improves visibility across channels, which helps advertisers learn more about their audience and adjust their campaigns accordingly.

“By working with Amazon Ads to consolidate our streaming TV investment, we can apply one audience strategy across our portfolio, and manage reach and frequency more effectively while better understanding what happens after an ad is seen,” Priyanti Telang, director of Amazon activation, retail media and digital shelf excellence for Philips North America, told me.

Using one buying platform also helps Philips speed up reporting.

Buying media and pulling reports from several platforms is “highly inefficient” because there is audience overlap, said Chris Conetta, director of omnichannel supply for Amazon Ads, so marketers “lose a lot of the incrementality you get when using one tool that can measure audiences across multiple touchpoints.”

That logic applies beyond just Amazon’s platform. Amazon (and other retailers, for that matter) can also attract brands seeking more purchase data to improve their performance and attribution, including on streaming TV.

Since TV is in its performance era, it’s not surprising that Philips was keen to prove streaming’s impact.

One of the clearest findings from its media consolidation effort, Telang said, is that “streaming can generate measurable intent.” After seeing the brand’s connected TV ads, more consumers searched online for Philips products by name, she said, and “that intent translated into purchases.”

Philips saw a 15x higher purchase rate among consumers who saw the ads on streaming TV than among consumers who only saw a Sponsored Ads placement for Philips online.

Conetta noted, however, that this increase was a result of customers seeing Philips ads across both streaming and on Amazon’s site. An Amazon executive would say that, but Conetta has a point. Industry research suggests that diversified ad formats can drive improved brand results.

Philips Sonicare’s experience also says something about streaming TV’s place in the marketing funnel, Telang said, “as a contributor to commercial performance as well as brand awareness.” Guess reach and performance complement each other like brushing and flossing.

In other words, brace yourselves (ha) to hear more about “full-funnel” advertising in CTV advertising discussions.

#7476. Hearst is working with creators to execute original content and brand deals on the fly

Hearst Communications has a long history of working alongside influencers, and it is bringing that effort into the current phase of the creator economy. A new venture called Hearst Creator Studios combines elements of a talent agency with the structure of a creator network to establish a unit that can deliver original content and branded media.

According to Adweek, Hearst’s new venture will be active across five of its editorial brands, including Cosmopolitan, Elle, and MotorTrend. More than 50 creators are involved, and Hearst is splitting them into two groups. So-called “creators at large” will be contracted to produce content, including at least seven original series. The rest of the creators will be “friends of the brand” who will be plugged into an internal, searchable platform that can be accessed by producers and brands.

Though Hearst is nearly 140 years old, it has never been shy about incorporating digital creators into its editorial brands. Its attempts to turn on that pipeline have evolved alongside the creator economy. A decade ago, Hearst invested in multi-channel networks to gain access to the creator lineups assembled therein. In 2020, its U.K. arm established an “influence network” meant to increase its social media presence. Other Hearst experiments have involved original programming, TikTok integrations, and Reddit-esque upvotes.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

Recently, brands have discovered an exciting new way to harness social media influence: Creator programs. That’s the name given to in-house networks that turn popular creators into brand spokespeople. After companies like Home Depot pioneered the concept, brands like Nat Geo have applied it to the realm of editorial content.

That being said, Hearst Magazines EVP and Global Chief Revenue Officer Lisa Ryan Howard told Adweek that the company’s Creator Studios is not a creator program. Instead, editors-in-chief handpick creator partners and appoint talent managers to work alongside those creators’ reps.

The result is a venture that operates most similarly to a talent agency. “Marketers want this because they want a curatorial eye on the creators,” Howard said, “as well as a one-stop shop.”

The early output from Hearst Creator Studios includes The Feelings Department, which comes from creators Izzy Perez and Emma Fuente and hits Cosmopolitan accounts in November. The plan is to increase the program’s output in 2027, when the 30-plus brands in Hearst’s editorial portfolio will gain access to a burgeoning network of creator partners.

#7473. Putting AI To Work At WSJ

The best AI use cases in ad sales aren’t flashy. Mostly, it’s about automating the tasks nobody wanted to do anyway.

That’s been the case at The Wall Street Journal, where AI is quietly taking over most of the busywork for the ad sales team, says Josh Stinchcomb, the Journal’s global CRO, on this week’s episode of AdExchanger Talks.

For example, what seller doesn’t know the frustration of trying to track down a stat buried somewhere in an old email thread or Slack channel when they’re trying to get ready for a meeting?

But now, the Journal’s sales team has access to an internal AI-powered search tool that does the digging for them. It can even recap whatever the seller last discussed with a particular prospect so they can walk into their meeting prepared and knowing exactly where the conversation left off.

“It’s really helpful for pulling from the information we have available to ourselves but isn’t always at our fingertips,” Stinchcomb says. “That’s been a great time-saver.”

There’s also a tool for digital ops that checks line items against ad creative and IOs and also handles taking campaign screenshots, which Stinchcomb describes as a decidedly “laborious and really unfun” task. The result, he says, is fewer botched campaign launches and less inventory lost to make-goods.

Right now, it takes a planner four or five hours to turn an RFP into a plan, Stinchcomb says, in part because they have to check inventory across multiple different systems. The Journal is testing a tool, however, that can read RFPs, look at past campaigns for similar audiences and build a recommended plan in about an hour.

With the team producing thousands of plans a year, that’s a lot of hours back in their lives. The time and effort saved is being redeployed toward larger million-dollar-plus RFPs, where Stinchcomb says the Journal’s win rate has gone up five percentage points. A wider rollout of the tool is planned for early next year.

“Bringing it all together is a great strategy,” he says. “It’s an efficient way to bring in chunks of revenue.”

But there’s one place where AI isn’t welcome, though, and that’s in the writing of branded content, which is a growing business for the Journal. WSJ Intelligence, its custom content studio, takes its cue from the Journal’s newsroom. The work might be “facilitated by these tools,” Stinchcomb says, “but not written by them.”

“AI is great at sort of rehashing what’s out there,” Stinchcomb says. “It’s not necessarily great at breaking news, as it were, or bringing a fresher perspective.”

Branded content has to be as interesting and engaging as anything else that’s out there competing for a reader’s attention.

And if it commits the sin of being boring or derivative, Stinchcomb says, then “[people] don’t read it, and I’m not getting paid.”

Also in this episode: Why less than 5% of the Journal’s digital ad revenue is programmatic, how WSJ Intelligence keeps its custom research credible, News Corp’s “woo and sue” approach to AI licensing deals and Stinchcomb’s past life as the singer in a “tragic emo-style” band in high school.

Elsewhere in the ranking, a one-time collaborator of MrBeast’s is making waves on his own. One of Latin America’s biggest creators has taken advantage of spooky season while tying in a cultural phenomenon that has had a consistent presence within our charts.

MrBeast isn’t involved in Vigevani’s biggest video of 2026, but a creepy clown is. After claiming to purchase the clown on the dark web, Vigevani used it as the primary prop in a multi-part series that drew inspiration from the smash-hit, YouTube-born franchise Backrooms.

Vigevani dropped his Backrooms-inspired series in the middle of spooky season, and that approach paid off. The ninth installment of the series, which arrived on November 11, was particular popular. It already has nearly 40 million views, and Vigevani has called it his biggest video of the year.

The culmination of Vigevani’s clown serial pushed him up to 27th place in the Global Top 50. He collected 413.1 million weekly views, increasing his YouTube traffic by 28% week-over-week in the process.

English-speaking consumers might think that clown horror is so ten years ago. Back in 2016, a viral clown craze turned into a veritable panic in the days surrounding Halloween. That experience convinced many that clowns are too creepy to belong at children’s parties.

In Latin America, however, clown content still has legs. One of the biggest channels in the region is El Payaso Plim Plim, a clown who isn’t afraid to remain kid-friendly. We’ve had regular Plim Plim sightings in our charts for years, and that trend has continued into 2026. There hasn’t been a week over the past six months in which Plim Plim has collected fewer than 250 million views.

Vigevani has found a clever way to apply that interest in clowns to a more adult audience. By leaning into the inherent horror of pale faces and colorful makeup, Vigevani has revived a decade-old craze and picked up tens of millions of views in the process.

I doubt Plim Plim, who appeals to young children, would approve of Vigevani’s recharacterization of clowns. But that’s what happens when you get your clown on the dark web — you don’t always get what you pay for.

#7467. Substack management firm Brigade snapped up by Hollywood’s Entertainment 360

Entertainment 360, the Hollywood talent and literary management company that reps celebrities like Margot Robbie and Julianne Moore, has acquired Brigade, a digital talent firm that specializes in Substack writers and podcasters.

As part of the deal, Brigade founder Max Stein will join Entertainment 360 as a Partner. He’ll bring with him Brigade’s team of managers and the firm’s ~40 clients, all of whom will keep their current representatives, he told The New York Times.

Among those clients are notable Substack writers Leandra Medine Cohen (a well-known fashion maven) and Emily Sundberg, who writes daily business newsletter Feed Me, as well as podcast host/creative consultant Chris Black and celebrity stylist Danielle Goldberg.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

Hollywood’s interest in creators has been the big buzz for a while, but that interest tends to zero in on moviemakers. Brigade’s clients–particularly its Substack contingent–are from other, oft-overlooked disciplines where digital talent and legacy entertainment could mesh.

“I’ve always been drawn to people with a singular point of view, whose work and ambitions don’t fit neatly into one category,” Stein, who got his start in fashion and launched Brigade in 2015, said in a statement. “Our clients have built remarkable careers by following their own taste and instincts, and our job has been to help them turn those ideas into lasting businesses.”

Entertainment 360 Partner Darin Friedman told The Hollywood Reporter that the worlds of digital and legacy entertainment “have collapsed a bit on each other.”

“YouTube is competing with Netflix, and Netflix is buying podcasts, and Disney is wanting to set meetings with comedians who want to develop TV shows,” he added.

In a separate statement, Entertainment 360’s Partners collectively said they’ve noticed “[t]he ways audiences discover and engage with entertainment have changed, and so have the needs of the talent building careers today.”

“Bringing Brigade into 360 expands what we can offer our clients and strengthens our ability to create extraordinary opportunities for artists across an increasingly diverse entertainment landscape,” they added.

Stein, meanwhile, told NYT that Brigade’s digital clients “are still attracted to some of the more legacy things.”

Sundberg took to LinkedIn to offer her own perspective on the deal.

“I’d be nervous if I were one of two groups of people–teams at the giant talent agencies like WME and United Talent Agency who aren’t spending time learning about the economics and opportunities of platforms like Substack; and Substack’s internal ad team, who needs to learn how to work with agencies like Entertainment 360 (and Spur and Amplifier and Alltogether) who already have deep relationships with advertisers,” she said.

Substack might be one step ahead there: As Digiday spotted today, Substack has a new job listing out for a U.S.-based Product Manager of Payments. The role’s description says the manager will handle gifting, retention offers, and improvement to payment and subscription experiences, along with advertising monetization–all with the (presumed) goal of getting creators paid more.

Substack already pumped up newsletter sponsorships earlier this year, debuting Creator Kits to help writers secure brand deals. Other creator-friendly adds to its service include a TikTok-style promo feed and a $20 million Creator Accelerator Fund.

360 and Brigade didn’t disclose financials of their acquisition, but we’re betting they both see potential gold in uniting across largely unexplored territory.

#7465. Canvas Worldwide’s Agentic Layer Helps Zillow Distinguish Real Renters From Dreamers

We’ve all been there: You look up a product out of sheer curiosity with no intent to actually spend money on it, and suddenly you’re inundated with ads for similar products.

The challenge for advertisers is distinguishing the passive browsers from the people with genuine purchase intent.

Zillow knows that challenge well. Its rental site often serves as a place for people to fantasize about their future home, even if they’re not actually looking to move.

“We are known for dreaming,” said Ravi Kandikonda, SVP of marketing for Zillow Group. But that’s not necessarily a bad thing. Welcoming the dreamers is a great way for Zillow to drive awareness of its brand and get potential future renters into its platform, Kandikonda added. From there, it’s a matter of striking a balance between building awareness and driving conversions.

That’s where Zillow turns to its media agency partner, Canvas Worldwide.

In September, Canvas announced a new division called ART Dept., which provides a collection of AI solutions to help brands and agencies optimize their campaign budgeting and pacing. Zillow is using ART Dept.’s AI agents to better separate the renters from the dreamers and tailor its marketing accordingly.

The “ART” in ART Dept. stands for “AI Applied Research and Technology.” (Though, if we’re being pedantic, wouldn’t that be AART – or AIART?)

Quibbles about acronyms aside, Canvas’ new division offers a mix of AI optimization features that are becoming commonplace for ad agencies and marketing platforms. Though, like other agentic platforms, Canvas says its differentiation comes from how it applies those optimizations to its agentic layer.

For example, offering a pacing dashboard is “table stakes” by now, rather than a distinguishing feature for an agency, said Sally Lee, SVP of programmatic and ART at Canvas.

But Canvas wanted to make its pacing dashboard “multidimensional” by connecting it with a budget source of truth and building an agentic layer on top of it, said Lee.

The agentic layer, called Talos, determines whether a campaign is underpacing or overpacing and optimizes for better performance. Before pushing the newly optimized campaign into the platform, a member of the Canvas team reviews and approves (or denies) it.

Canvas can “pick and choose from different search and behavioral categories” to optimize against, said Lee. In Zillow’s case, that might include whether a user is researching renter’s insurance or looking into moving truck rentals.

Canvas gets those behavioral signals through its data partnerships, including its MCP connection to predictive audience targeting company Dstillery.

Access to behavioral data has helped Zillow reach more specific audiences and be smarter about exactly where and when to target them, said Kandikonda.

For instance, targeting multifamily renters in Seattle using a generic, off-the-shelf “multifamily apartment buildings” audience only goes so far, he said. “I need to know when they are on a particular platform” to bid for that audience at the right moment with the right content, he added.

Dstillery’s audience modeling predicts which websites the target audience will visit and when based on real behavioral data. And Canvas’ AI can help surface audience and behavioral overlaps that might have previously gone overlooked by its team.

Canvas’ reliance on data-backed reasoning was a major draw for Zillow when the two first started working together in 2023, Kandikonda said, and it continues to be a major focus of ART Dept.

The goal behind the new product suite is to save media teams time figuring out what media is performing and how much to spend on different audience segments.

Increasing ROI is important for any brand. But it’s particularly important within the real estate market, Kandikonda said, as marketing dollars are constrained and the entire industry “is bouncing around the box.”

So, while Zillow appreciates its dreamer audience, it’s feeling the same pressure most brands are to focus on lower-funnel conversions, such as “actual movers,” Kandikonda said.

That’s part of the reason off-the-shelf renter audiences weren’t cutting it for Zillow’s ads business, he added.

An off-the-shelf audience may indicate people who are interested in renting more broadly, he said, but ART was able to select for people who were actively in the process of planning a move. And more precise targeting means better lower-funnel ad performance.

From Zillow’s perspective, the biggest change from using Canvas’ ART Dept. is the results, rather than the process. After all, the AI tools are used by the Canvas team, rather than by Zillow.

Zillow just tells Canvas what outcome it wants to achieve. Canvas then translates the desired outcome into a scorecard that weights different goals and metrics within the interoperable tech infrastructure that powers the ART Dept., which is called +Suite.

From there, Canvas’ Audience+ product (which is similar to a data management platform) connects to data partners and the Talos AI agent to build custom audiences. Finally, Talos activates and optimizes the campaign.

The system creates an ongoing feedback loop, said Canvas’ Lee: “Build an audience, activate it, see how it’s performing against what that client cares about and identify where to make changes to drive a better outcome.”

#7459. Among social media ads, short-form video drives the most actions

Social media advertising continues to grow, but not all ads are created equal. The ad tech company DoubleVerify has released its 2026 Global Insights Report, a dispatch that identifies YouTube and Facebook — and their respective short-form formats — as dominant forces in the social media marketing landscape.

DoubleVerify compiled its report by collecting responses from 22,000 consumers and 2,020 marketers, spanning regions like North America, Latin America, EMEA, and Asia-Pacific. One thing those global respondents can agree on is their appreciation of YouTube. Google’s video hub is the most-used platform across all age groups and regions, with 95% of all respondents claiming to use it.

Those users are also warming up to YouTube’s ad ecosystem. Half of the respondents said they would take action based on YouTube ads; that was the highest percentage among all measured platforms. Facebook came in second on that axis (49%), followed by Instagram (42%) and TikTok (38%).

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

Other platforms are lagging behind in terms of actionable ads, and DoubleVerify’s findings suggest a big difference between those four industry leaders and their competitors. YouTube, Facebook, Instagram, and TikTok are four platforms where short-form media has been widely adopted, and 38% of DoubleVerify respondents said that short-form ads inspire them to take action. That was 7% higher than the next ad format on the list (long-form video pre-rolls, at 31%).

The ubiquity of short-form video is one factor that seems to be making ads more palatable across social media. Since the release of DoubleVerify’s 2025 Global Insights Report, 8% more consumers have decided that social media platforms are suitable locations for ads. YouTube, at 72%, was deemed the most valid platform for those spots.

DoubleVerify’s report shows that social media spend is paying off across multiple platforms, but marketers must still pick and choose as they allocate their ad dollars. As we saw with the Pew Research Center’s recent survey of American social media habits, usage data can vary wildly depending on demographic filters like age, gender, and household income.

That assertion held true in the DoubleVerify report, in which TikTok ranked as the third most-used platform among 18-to-24-year-olds but didn’t crack the top five among the 65+ set. And most platforms skewed male worldwide, but 8% more female respondents use Pinterest compared to men.

The global scope of DoubleVerify’s report adds another wrinkle to the conversation. In the Asia-Pacific region, for example, 56% of respondents said that influencer activity “somewhat to significantly” impacted purchase decisions. In North America, that statistic is only 39%. So if marketers want to ensure that their social media activity inspires action, they should deploy their budgets wisely.

#7455. Tubi wants more creator content. The Kickstarter-backed “Fandom Fund” is here to help.

As Tubi looks to bring more creators to its shores, it is helping them solve a prevalent problem by providing easier access to capital. That’s the gist of the Tubi x Kickstarter Fandom Fund, which unites a Fox-owned streaming service and a 17-year-old crowdfunding platform.

The Fandom Fund follows up last year’s FilmStream Collective, a partnership between Tubi and Kickstarter that delivered support to more than 20 independent films. The new collab between the companies will function similarly; Tubi will throw its weight behind active Kickstarter campaigns, which it will distribute exclusively.

Tubi won’t just pick any Kickstarter project; instead, as it has done with its other incubator programs, it will hone in on the genres that have the widest appeal among its 110 million monthly active users. The categories fitting that description include horror, YA, Black entertainment, true crime, LGBTQ+, comedy, and reality.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

For Kickstarter, the Fandom Fund represents an increasing commitment to the creator economy. It is part of the three-month-old Culture Fund, which builds on Kickstarter’s enduring status as a key tool for indie artists. In 2024 alone, the platform generated over $700 million of fundraising across more than 35,000 projects.

Indie creators don’t always get distribution deals with brand-name platforms, but Tubi is eager to support the next generation of storytellers — whom it believes are just as capable as traditional TV voices. To that end, Tubi has premiered a handful of shows and movies led by social media standouts. One of the projects in the Fandom Fund will get a similar treatment by receiving additional backing, allowing it to be developed into a full-length series or feature film.

“We believe great talent can come from anywhere,” said Tubi GM of Creator Programs and EVP of Business Development Rich Bloom in a statement. “The Fandom Fund gives emerging storytellers the resources to bring those ambitious ideas to life on a bigger canvas while preserving the creative voice, vision and ownership that made their work resonate.”

Kickstarter will provide updates about the Fandom Fund through its film-focused newsletter. Participation in the fund requires an active campaign, so if you want Tubi’s backing, get your crowdfunding game on.

#7452. Sick of pirates and freebooters? Meta brings its “content protection” tool to Instagram.

Pirated content has been an issue for Meta for so long that it was still known as Facebook when creators first fought back against so-called “freebooters.” To combat unauthorized reuploads, Meta brought a “content protection” tool to Facebook last year. Now, Instagram creators are getting access to that resource as well.

“Eligible creators” on Instagram can now enroll for access to the management system that was previously limited to Facebook. Like Facebook’s video rights manager, which was itself adapted from previous services like YouTube’s Content ID, the content protection tool uses fingerprinting technology to scan for uploads that are identical to an enrolled creator’s video.

Once a match is detected, Instagrammers can respond in one of four different ways: They can track the reupload (that’s the default option), request for it to be hidden, require the reuploader to add a credit link, or release their claim on the infringing video. Notably, creators cannot receive monetization through the reposts, as is possible through services like Content ID.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

Meta has positioned itself as a champion of original, non-repetitive content. It updated Instagram’s algorithm, providing more visibility for creators who share their own work. Financial penalties for serial reuploaders came to Facebook in 2025, and further penalties arrived on Instagram this year.

Other platforms have followed Meta’s lead. YouTube cracked down on “mass-produced or repetitive” content in 2025. Earlier this year, Google’s video hub clarified that creators aren’t able to monetize “generic” uploads. Anything “unsatisfying or off-putting” — i.e. the sort of slop you’d expected a generative AI model to spit out — faced similar repercussions.

The link between unoriginal reuploads and AI slop is undeniable. Traditional studios have urged platforms to crack down on channels that use AI to steal from artists rather than executing original concepts. Those demands have led to new rules across TikTok, YouTube, Facebook, and Instagram.

By bringing content protection to Instagram, Meta is setting itself up to take further action against AI slop in the future. An introductory post explains that “we’re also exploring different ways to limit the reach of content and profiles that use AI tools to post this type of content repeatedly,” so stay tuned for that if you’re sick of low-effort AI posts.

#7449. As Netflix and Disney sniff around, YouTube hypes its creators’ “world-class, studio-quality” programming at L.A. Premieres event

Tonight, YouTube brought back its film-festival-style event, Creator Premieres, to showcase a new batch of “world-class, studio-quality creator programming” coming exclusively to its platform.

Last year’s Creator Premieres–the first YouTube held–took place at New York City’s historic screening space Metrograph and showed off projects from creators like Ms. Rachel, Brave Wilderness, Dhar Mann, Deestroying, and Cleo Abram.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

This year’s edition was hosted by House Guest‘s Scott Evans at The Hollywood Roosevelt in L.A., and highlighted upcoming projects from YouTube OGs and greats like Emma Chamberlain, Nick DiGiovanni, Lilly Singh, Wesley Wang, Grace Reiter, and more.

Google President Sean Downey took the stage to highlight YouTube’s continued dominance on TV screens, and gave a nod to participating creators for fueling the UGC machine that keeps viewers coming back to YouTube–on TVs and across other devices.

Of course, he also appealed to advertisers in the same breath, reminding them that this “world-class” content is what they could be marketing alongside, if they cough up the cash to Google.

“YouTube creators are not just shaping modern culture, they are redefining the entire entertainment landscape. This slate of shows demonstrates how creators are commanding primetime attention on the big screen and building unmatched fan loyalty,” Downey said. “For brands, this isn’t about buying thirty seconds of ad space; it’s about moving past standard commercial breaks and partnering directly with the storytellers who are defining modern culture.”

YouTube has spent years at the top of TV watch time charts–a fact that really gets under the skin of competitor Netflix. Up till recently, though, Netflix’s main response to this irritant was talking a lot of sh*t about YouTube and occasionally signing back catalog deals with view-drivers like Ms. Rachel and CoComelon.

But in the last 12 months, something’s shifted. Netflix has begun tapping creators like Salish Matter, Alan Chikin Chow, and the Stokes Twins not for back catalog agreements, but for development deals–deals which result in exclusive original programming that won’t appear on YouTube.

And YouTube’s not happy about it. The platform has been offering creators money, including production financing and sweet ad deals, in exchange for turning down offers from Netflix. Conversely, creators who decide to sign with Netflix are put on YouTube’s naughty list, and denied perks like revenue shares from primo ad deals.

(That being said, Netflix-friendly creators aren’t entirely blacklisted. DiGiovanni signed a catalog crossposting deal with Netflix in July, and was still one of the headline creators at tonight’s showcase.)

The point we’re making here is this: With Netflix–and Disney–sniffing around, YouTube has more incentive than ever to hype up its creators and their projects on a big stage.

Nick DiGiovanni | Chef | New series live now on a dedicated YouTube channel

Chef Nick DiGiovanni, the creator behind the world’s largest food YouTube channel, launches Chef (@Chef) – a new series from his production company, Knife Drop Studios. After reaching billions of viewers through his global culinary adventures (@NickDiGiovanni) and step-by-step recipes (@NicksKitchen), DiGiovanni is now turning the camera solely toward fellow professional chefs, offering an unfiltered look inside kitchens around the globe. From Michelin-starred restaurants and hidden street food gems showcased in full-length episodes, to POV recipes in short-form episodes, Chef puts viewers in the shoes of the people behind the scenes, offering a unique, captivating perspective for everyone from the culinary obsessed to the simply curious. You can view the first full-length episode, “Inside the World’s #1 Pizza Restaurant” now, only on YouTube, along with the first short-form POV episode, “Butter Chicken Shawarma”. New short-form POV episodes will debut daily across Nick’s newly-launched @Chef channel with full-length episodes rolling out throughout 2026-27 exclusively on YouTube.

Morgan Jay | Music Therapy with Morgan Jay | New series premieres Nov. 18 on Jay’s YouTube channel

Music Therapy is an original YouTube series developed and produced by viral comedian and musician Morgan Jay and Ty Stafford of Austin-based creative agency Hello Party, financed by Live Nation Studios. In each episode, Jay plays musical therapist to a celebrity guest, blending unscripted conversation and improv with live songwriting before the pair close with an original song they create together. The result lands somewhere between a talk show, a comedy special and a live concert. The first season features Kam Patterson, Ron Funches, Mara Wilson, Brennan Lee Mulligan, Yung Gravy, Matt Friend, Abbey Romeo, Mark Smalls, Tony Jefferson, ASHBY, Josh Johnson and Mandal Mann. Music Therapy was created by Morgan Jay and Ty Stafford (Hello Party) and is directed by Stafford. Brooke Schley serves as showrunner and co-writes the series with Jay. Executive producers are Graham Sicalowski, Robin Rapino, Stella Bulochnikov, Brooke Schley and Matt Sadeghian.

Emma Chamberlain | What Are You Waiting For? | New series premieres early 2027 on Chamberlain’s channel

Emma Chamberlain doesn’t like waiting in line – and wants to understand more about people who do. In this new ongoing series, what starts as an investigation of New York City’s most frequented lines unspools into a thoughtful and expansive meditation on subcultures, fandoms, and what makes our modern world tick. At once whimsical, profound and provocative, and underpinned by Emma’s singular POV, What Are You Waiting For? is a hilarious cultural commentary that not only asks what people are waiting for – but why. The series is executive produced by two-time Emmy and Golden Globe winner Joe Lewis, with Amplify Pictures (Fleabag, 100 Foot Wave) serving as the co-studio and production company.

Grace Reiter | Twilight (but better) | New parody film premieres Feb. 18 on Reiter’s channel

Comedian, writer, and actor Grace Reiter (Saturday Night Live) is expanding her comedic universe with Twilight (but better), her second unscripted parody film. Reiter first made waves with her viral sketches and The Hunger Games (but better), which launched on YouTube in November 2025 and has garnered more than 18 million views. Now, alongside her work on SNL and her Netflix series Minimum Wage, Reiter brings her signature blend of spontaneous comedy, sharp satire, and irreverent humor to one of the most iconic franchises of a generation. Twilight (but better) is produced by But Better Productions. Grace Reiter serves as director with Andie Schlenker and Anderson Appleby as producers, and Cindy Schlenker as co-producer.

Aryna Sabalenka | Aryna’s Arena: Unfiltered | New series premieres spring 2027 on Sabalenka’s channel

She’s the most dominant tennis player on the planet; and the world can’t look away. Aryna Sabalenka has spent years letting us watch her win. Now cameras follow her everywhere press passes don’t go. A Gucci ambassador designing her own $250K diamond necklace, a bride-to-be planning a wedding while living out of a suitcase for 300+ days a year, a daughter flying home to Belarus between slams, Aryna is building an empire in real time with the whole world watching. From UltraBoom Media, the creators of OFF DAY, a team led by Producers and Creatives from Anthony Bourdain: Parts Unknown, Aryna’s Arena: Unfiltered is an evolution and expansion of Aryna Sabalenka’s YouTube series (Aryna’s Arena).
